sub_topics: Televised testimony of Ruby Tuason before Senate blue ribbon committee has been hailed as grand 'slam dunk', only 'lay-up', and winning 'three-point buzzer-beater'
These street-smart assessments of how former Malacañang social queen pinned down her longtime family friend-senator are, of course, familiar to basketball diehards
After effusive sports lingo, assessments turned more serious from 'sabotage' and 'worthless' to 'sufficient proof of conspiracy... enough to convict' another senator
CJP thinks all these descriptions should be understood in their proper context
Tuason's testimony was not about basketball or criminal law
Rather, her appearance was about assisting Senate in crafting or amending legislation to stop graft
For example, committee could, as result of its hearing, sponsor bill on how to prevent suspects from leaving country
And how to proceed against those who managed to sneak out, without violating their constitutional rights
Or how to make it easier for prosecutors to indict high officials, especially legislators
Or how to find novel ways to prevent and penalize new forms of graft
Tuason did not testify in Senate to defend herself in plunder charge thrown at her by DOJ
Neither was it to implicate or protect any of her corespondents
It would be unfair to assess her testimony to show anyone's complicity in any crime
These are simply not purposes of Senate hearing
True, congressional investigation can sometimes engender belief that crime had been committed and that certain individuals are possibly guilty thereof
But Congress cannot indict them in court, much less pass upon their guilt and sentence them to jail
It may, however, recommend their prosecution to DOJ or Office of Ombudsman
But discretion on whether to indict them belongs solely to these two latter offices
Criminal procedures are more exacting than congressional investigations
First, information (or charge sheet) must be filed in proper court that has jurisdiction over it
Second, information must be clearly and accurately worded to comply with constitutional right of accused 'to be informed of nature and cause of accusation against him'
Thus, information must set out:
(a) names of accused
(b) designation of offense given by statute
(c) specific acts or omissions constituting crime coached in ordinary and concise language
(d) approximate date of offense
(e) place where it was committed
As rule, information must charge only one offense
In short, information must contain 'essential elements' of crime which must be worded clearly 'to enable a person of common understanding to know what offense is being charged'
To empower him or her to prepare his or her defense
Unless foregoing safeguards are put in place, guilt or innocence cannot be deduced from testimony of any witness
Reason is that testimony must be received and admitted only when it is both 'relevant' and 'material' to specific crime charged
Furthermore, questions must be propounded properly and clearly, without misleading or confusing witness
Finally and most importantly, adverse party must be given opportunity to cross-examine witness

Despite many scientific advances in crime detection and prosecution, old-fashioned cross-examination conducted by skilled lawyer is still best-known way of testing truthfulness and credibility of witnesses
Unless subjected to cross-examination, testimony is hearsay and cannot be used to convict or prejudice accused
In congressional investigations, questions are sometimes recklessly asked without sufficient predicate (or basis)
Thereby eliciting unresponsive, incomplete or wrong answers
Moreover, resource persons (they are not called 'witnesses') are not cross-examined by adverse parties
Because there are no adverse parties in legislative inquiries
Point is: unless safeguards in criminal proceeding are observed, testimony given in congressional probes cannot be used to indict or incriminate third persons
Or for that matter, to free the guilty
This is why Supreme Court has restricted (no longer absolutely banned) live coverage of trials
At bottom, street-smart assessments of Ruby Tuason's performance should be understood in their congressional context rather than as legal opinions on criminal liability
Let us remember that her testimony was taken without any specific criminal indictment
Without any safeguard for rights of putative accused
And without benefit of cross-examination
In court of public opinion, these open and much-publicized congressional hearings can besmirch reputations, cause sleeplessness and anxiety
And lead to severe consequences to conscience-stricken or mentally unbalanced
Some politicians may lose their charisma and political clout
Others may even go, as some have gone, to extreme of hara-kiri or suicide
In courts of law, criminal guilt or innocence is not determined by passing passion of political thicket
But by serene, quiet and rule-based trial speedily conducted by competent, independent and trustworthy judges
Assisted by skilled, dedicated and ethical lawyers

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the second installment of his two-part Ruby-Tuason arc (after A425 Feb 16 on her criminal liability), opening with one of his most memorable rhetorical devices -- basketball metaphors. The televised testimony of Ruby Tuason before the Senate blue ribbon committee has been hailed as a grand 'slam dunk,' only a 'lay-up,' and a winning 'three-point buzzer-beater' -- these street-smart assessments of how the former Malacañang social queen pinned down her longtime family friend-senator are, of course, familiar to basketball diehards. Purpose of testimony: after the effusive sports lingo, the assessments turned more serious from 'sabotage' and 'worthless' to 'sufficient proof of conspiracy... enough to convict' another senator. CJ thinks all these descriptions should be understood in their proper context. Tuason's testimony was not about basketball or criminal law -- rather, her appearance was about assisting the Senate in crafting or amending legislation to stop graft. For example, the committee could, as a result of its hearing, sponsor a bill on how to prevent suspects from leaving the country, and how to proceed against those who managed to sneak out, without violating their constitutional rights. Or how to make it easier for prosecutors to indict high officials, especially legislators. Or how to find novel ways to prevent and penalize new forms of graft. Tuason did not testify in the Senate to defend herself in the plunder charge thrown at her by the DOJ; neither was it to implicate or protect any of her corespondents; it would be unfair to assess her testimony to show anyone's complicity in any crime -- these are simply not the purposes of the Senate hearing. True, congressional investigation can sometimes engender the belief that a crime had been committed and that certain individuals are possibly guilty thereof -- but Congress cannot indict them in court, much less pass upon their guilt and sentence them to jail; it may, however, recommend their prosecution to the DOJ or the Office of the Ombudsman, but the discretion on whether to indict them belongs solely to these two latter offices. More exacting: criminal procedures are more exacting than congressional investigations. First, the information (or charge sheet) must be filed in the proper court that has jurisdiction over it; and second, the information must be clearly and accurately worded to comply with the constitutional right of the accused 'to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation against him.' Thus, the information must set out (a) the names of the accused, (b) the designation of the offense given by the statute, (c) the specific acts or omissions constituting the crime coached in ordinary and concise language, (d) the approximate date of the offense, and (e) the place where it was committed; as a rule, an information must charge only one offense. In short, the information must contain the 'essential elements' of the crime which must be worded clearly 'to enable a person of common understanding to know what offense is being charged,' to empower him or her to prepare his or her defense. Unless the foregoing safeguards are put in place, guilt or innocence cannot be deduced from the testimony of any witness -- the reason is that the testimony must be received and admitted only when it is both 'relevant' and 'material' to the specific crime charged; furthermore, the questions must be propounded properly and clearly, without misleading or confusing the witness. Finally and most importantly, the adverse party must be given the opportunity to cross-examine the witness -- despite the many scientific advances in crime detection and prosecution, the old-fashioned cross-examination conducted by a skilled lawyer is still the best-known way of testing the truthfulness and credibility of witnesses; unless subjected to cross-examination, testimony is hearsay and cannot be used to convict or prejudice the accused. In congressional investigations, questions are sometimes recklessly asked without sufficient predicate (or basis), thereby eliciting unresponsive, incomplete or wrong answers; moreover, resource persons (they are not called 'witnesses') are not cross-examined by adverse parties, because there are no adverse parties in legislative inquiries. The point is: unless the safeguards in a criminal proceeding are observed, the testimony given in congressional probes cannot be used to indict or incriminate third persons, or for that matter, to free the guilty; this is why the SC has restricted (no longer absolutely banned) live coverage of trials. Context and complications: at bottom, the street-smart assessments of Ruby Tuason's performance should be understood in their congressional context rather than as legal opinions on criminal liability -- let us remember that her testimony was taken without any specific criminal indictment, without any safeguard for the rights of the putative accused, and without the benefit of cross-examination. In the court of public opinion, these open and much-publicized congressional hearings can besmirch reputations, cause sleeplessness and anxiety, and lead to severe consequences to the conscience-stricken or mentally unbalanced -- some politicians may lose their charisma and political clout; others may even go, as some have gone, to the extreme of hara-kiri or suicide. In the courts of law, criminal guilt or innocence is not determined by the passing passion of the political thicket, but by a serene, quiet and rule-based trial speedily conducted by competent, independent and trustworthy judges, assisted by skilled, dedicated and ethical lawyers.
